name: Central Suriname Nature Reserve
blurb: Pristine Guiana rainforest where jaguars, harpy eagles and fruit-eaters shape the forest.

tip.title: Remove the agoutis
tip.text: Agoutis eat and bury large seeds and feed jaguars, ocelots and harpy eagles. Set Red-rumped agouti to -100% and watch the cats and eagles, and the trees that rely on it.

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage: Central Suriname Nature Reserve

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Light is scarce on the dark forest floor, so canopy trees capture most of it and shade the layers below.
Heavy year-round rain feeds the rivers and rapids of the Coppename watershed and keeps the lowland forest moist.
Old, weathered tropical soils hold few nutrients, so the forest relies on fast recycling of fallen leaves and wood.
Break down leaf litter, wood and dead animals, returning nutrients to the soil for roots to take up again.
Cut fresh leaves and carry them below ground to grow the fungus they feed on, making them major forest herbivores.
A fruit-eating bat that feeds on Piper fruit and spreads its seeds through the forest at night.
A rodent that eats seeds, pulp and fruit. It buries seeds, so it can help plants spread.
A pig-like forest mammal that forages in groups on fruit, seeds and roots. Jaguars hunt it.
A medium-sized forest cat that hunts rodents like agoutis and other small to mid-sized animals.
A large forest scavenger that finds carcasses, including those left by big predators such as jaguars.
The largest cat of the Americas and the top ground predator here. It hunts peccaries and agoutis among many prey.
A huge forest eagle that hunts sloths and monkeys in the canopy, including spider monkeys and capuchins.
